entries.title: Sizing Lakebase Search: lessons from a real app and 4 million passages
entries.summary: Slide Hub is an internal Databricks app. Field engineers use it to find and reuse...
entries.content:
• Lakebase Search runs vector and BM25 keyword search as Postgres extensions inside the application database, so developers get hybrid search without maintaining a separate search system or a second transaction path.
  • Benchmarks show that sizing the Local File Cache to roughly match the vector index keeps 95~98% of pages in memory, dropping warm vector latency to single-digit milliseconds, while reducing the candidate pool from 1,000 to 200 preserves 90.5% of top-10 results at one-third the page reads.
  • Lakebase Postgres bills compute only while it runs, and a 14-minute load test serving 109k requests used just $0.02 of Lakebase Postgres compute, making a $31~40/month always-on 0.5 CU floor the recommended production baseline to avoid cold starts.

Slide Hub is an internal Databricks app. Field engineers use it to find and reuse slides from about 700 internal presentations: event talks, product decks, and architecture decks. A search bar finds single slides by meaning and by keyword, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server gives AI agents the same search. The app stores its slides, votes, search telemetry, and change history in Lakebase Postgres. We use Slide Hub as the baseline to benchmark Lakebase Postgres. It is a real app with a real use case and real users, so its numbers show how the database behaves under an actual workload.

This post is for developers and architects who build apps on Databricks and want search inside the app's own Lakebase Postgres database. It assumes that you know SQL and the basics of PostgreSQL. If you plan a search bar or an agent tool on Lakebase Postgres, the numbers below help you choose the compute size before you go to production.

This post shows how Slide Hub runs search inside Lakebase Postgres, what limits it under load, what it costs, and how Lakebase Search behaves from 1M to 4M rows of a public corpus.

Lakebase Search became generally available in September. It is a set of Postgres extensions, so it runs next to the application tables. The app does not copy data to a separate search system. The developer does not maintain a second transaction path.

Two 

CREATE EXTENSION
statements enable the components. 
lakebase_vector
stores embeddings, vectors of numbers that represent the meaning of a text, and supports the 
lakebase_ann
index for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. 
lakebase_text
supports the 
lakebase_bm25
index for BM25, a standard method that ranks text by the query words it contains. 
lakebase_tokenizer
is optional. The ANN index uses IVF partitioning, which groups similar vectors so a query reads only a few groups, and RaBitQ quantization, which compresses each vector to about 1 bit per dimension. BM25 scores text with the <@> operator.

Slide Hub’s 23k slide rows sit in the same serverless Lakebase Postgres instance as the votes, telemetry, change history, previews, and both indexes. The app reads the data and the indexes inside one connection and one permission model.

Slide Hub runs hybrid search. It combines vector search, which finds slides with a similar meaning to the query, and BM25 keyword search, which finds slides that contain the query words. Each method returns a short list of its best matches, the candidates. One SQL statement carries the whole ranking policy. It ranks each candidate list, fuses the two rankings, applies the app filters, and joins the votes. Search and app logic share one connection, one set of grants, and one commit.

Slide Hub takes 200 candidates from each method. It fuses the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) at k=60: a slide scores 1/(60 + its rank) in each list, and the two scores add. A similarity gate of 0.70 rejects vector matches that are too far from the query to be useful for this embedding model. Title tiers add weight when the query matches a slide title. Notes receive weight 0.5. Scope filters restrict the result to assets the user has permission to see.

A search request uses two separate computes, and either one can set the limit.

Lakebase Postgres compute runs the database. Lakebase Postgres sizes it in Compute Units (CU). One CU allocates about 2 GB of RAM to the database, with its share of CPU and local SSD. A compute autoscales between a minimum and a maximum size from 0.5 CU to 64 CU, and the maximum can be at most 16 CU above the minimum. Fixed-size computes go up to 112 CU, and computes up to 32 CU can scale to zero.Postgres stores tables and indexes in 8 KB pages. Lakebase Postgres keeps recently read pages in a Local File Cache (LFC) on the compute. The cache grows with the CU size and can use up to 75% of the compute's memory. A page that is not in the cache comes from storage, which takes longer.

Databricks Apps compute runs the Slide Hub web server. Its size is fixed per app. A MEDIUM app has up to 2 vCPU and 6 GB of memory, and a LARGE app has up to 4 vCPU and 12 GB. Slide Hub runs one app instance. Each Python worker process in it holds a pool of 8 database connections, so 2 workers open at most 16 connections and 4 workers open at most 32.

For each request, the app embeds the query text, sends one SQL statement to Lakebase Postgrse, and returns the result. To find the limit, the test changes one side at a time. It pins Lakebase Postgres at one CU size and changes the app, or it keeps the app and changes the CU size. A load generator simulates users that send search requests, and it raises the number of users in steps. The list shows requests per second and the median latency (p50) at 500 users for each Lakebase Postgres size and app size.

  • 1 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 196 req/s, p50 1.8 s
  • 0.5 to 1 CU, LARGE app with 4 workers: 193 req/s, p50 1.6 s
  • 2 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 201 req/s, p50 1.8 s
  • 4 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 219 req/s, p50 1.6 s
  • 8 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 336 req/s, p50 1.0 s
  • 16 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 349 req/s, p50 1.0 s
  • 16 CU, LARGE app with 4 workers: at least 662 req/s, p50 343 ms

Up to 4 CU, Lakebase is the limit. A LARGE app with twice the workers and connections adds nothing at 1 CU. At 1 CU the search statement averaged 146 ms and read 14.9M pages from storage, with a file cache of 1.5 GB. At 8 CU it averaged 34 ms, with a cache of 12 GB, and throughput rose about 50%.

From 8 CU, the app is the limit. 16 CU with the same MEDIUM app adds only 4%, and its database connections sit mostly idle. A LARGE app with 4 workers at 16 CU reaches at least 662 req/s, and there the load generator was the limit. Size the query first. Then scale Lakebase Postgres until the app workers are the limit, and then scale the app.

Takeaway: Find the limit before you scale. Below 8 CU, add Lakebase Postgres CU. From 8 CU, give the app more workers.

The connection pool is still necessary. At 50 users the app reached 45 req/s and 2.4 s p95 without the pool, and 85 req/s and 0.7 s p95 with it. The embedding cache made no measurable difference under load.

The candidate limit sets the number of pages a query touches. On a cold cache, that number sets the latency. Slide Hub shipped with 1,000 candidates per method. The docs pattern uses 40. The candidate-limit experiment changed only candidate_limit and measured 20 public queries in three states. Cold is the first query after the compute scaled to zero, with an empty cache. First-touch is the first run of a query on an awake compute. Repeat is the same query run again, with its pages in the cache. Pages touched counts the pages a query reads from any source. Top-10 overlap is the share of the top 10 results that match the result at 1,000 candidates.

  • 40 candidates: cold 127 ms, first-touch 13 ms, repeat 5.0 ms. Touches 5,655 pages. Top-10 overlap 74.5%.
  • 100 candidates: cold 240 ms, first-touch 16 ms, repeat 7.9 ms. Touches 7,355 pages. Top-10 overlap 89%.
  • 200 candidates: cold 387 ms, first-touch 24 ms, repeat 11.7 ms. Touches 10,401 pages. Top-10 overlap 90.5%.
  • 1,000 candidates: cold 740 ms, first-touch 109 ms, repeat 35.3 ms. Touches 28,972 pages. Top-10 overlap 100% (the reference).

At 200 candidates, 90.5% of the top 10 stays the same, and the reported number of matches is 81% of the number at 1,000 candidates. Users rarely page past 200 results, so Slide Hub now ships 200. Measured end to end from a job in the same cloud region as the app, a cold search at 200 candidates took 2.9 s, and a repeat search took 40 ms. The cold time has two parts. The connection waits about 1 s while the endpoint wakes up. Then each query reads its pages from storage until the cache warms. The first query on a new connection also pays about 75 ms of planning.

Takeaway: Keep the candidate pool small. 200 candidates keep 90.5% of the top 10 results, read about a third of the pages of 1,000 candidates, and halve the cold latency.

The scale tests use MIRACL English, a passage corpus built from Wikipedia. The full corpus has 32,893,221 passages. We embedded it with gte-large-en-v1.5, a 1024-dimension open model, the same size as the Slide Hub embeddings. We self-hosted the model on one A10G GPU at 379 passages per second. The whole corpus took 2.95 GPU-hours, against $48.87 for the same work on a model-serving endpoint. The GPU vectors matched the endpoint vectors (mean cosine 1.0000, minimum 0.9978).

We built three subsets: 1M, 2M, and 4M passages. The lakebase_ann index grew with the corpus: 5.8 GB at 1M, 11.5 GB at 2M, 23.0 GB at 4M. A binary COPY loaded all 4M rows in 19 minutes at 8 CU.

Lakebase Postgres holds about 1.6 GB of file cache per CU. Scale raises one question: what happens when the index is larger than the cache? Each test cell is one corpus size at one CU size, so the cache is a known fraction of the index. We call that fraction the cache ratio: cache size divided by vector index size. A ratio of 1.0 means the index just fits. The hit rate is the share of the pages a query reads that do not come from storage.

We ran three query mixes against each cell. The uniform mix sends a new title every time and never repeats, the worst case for a cache. The skewed mix draws from a pool of 20,000 titles with a Zipf distribution, a common model for search traffic. The cold mix runs the first queries right after a wake-up, when the cache is empty. Before the uniform and skewed measurements, a warm-up runs the same mix until the hit rate stops changing. We call the results after the warm-up warm.

The hit rate depends on the cache ratio. The corpus size does not change it: the 2M and 4M points fall on one curve. At a ratio of 0.07 the skewed mix hit 45% of its pages in cache. At 0.57 it hit 86%. At 1.14, where the index just fits, it hit 97%. The uniform mix sits a few points lower, because it reuses nothing.

That gives a sizing rule. Measure your index size, pick a CU size for the cache ratio you want, and read the hit rate off the curve. The ratio works across corpus sizes, so a test at 2M predicts the behavior at 4M.

Takeaway: Size the cache from the vector index, not from the row count. A cache about as large as the index serves 95% to 98% of the pages without storage.

Warm vector p50 fell from 187 ms at a ratio of 0.07 to 4 ms at a ratio of 2.3. Hybrid search stayed near 800 ms until the ratio approached 1, then dropped to 33 ms. The keyword half of the hybrid query reads the most pages, so it gains the most from a full cache.

Takeaway: Vector search takes 160 to 230 ms while the cache holds less than a third of the index, and 11 to 23 ms once the whole index fits.

A miss is one 8 KB Postgres page that is not in the Local File Cache. In the vector index, one page holds one or two embeddings. One page read from storage costs a fixed amount of time. Across every measured query, execution time grows by about 252 microseconds per missed page for vector search and 316 for hybrid. A query that misses 2,000 pages pays about half a second. A full cache removes almost all the misses. This is why the cache ratio sets the latency: it sets how many pages each query reads from storage.

Takeaway: Each page from storage adds about 0.3 ms. Multiply the storage misses per query by 0.3 ms to estimate what the cache saves you.

Hold the cache ratio near 1.0 and change the corpus size. Warm vector latency stayed between 11 and 23 ms from 1M to 4M. Warm hybrid latency stayed near 276 ms. The cold queries, which read from storage, grew with the corpus: a cold vector query went from 44 ms at 1M to 133 ms at 4M, and a cold hybrid query reached 911 ms at 4M.

This is the honest form of “you do not need the whole index in memory”: you do not, because the architecture keeps compute memory flat. RaBitQ stores about 1 bit per dimension, 32 times smaller than float32, and IVF reads only a few partitions per query. The index is storage-backed, so compute can be small or scale to zero. The queries that miss the cache pay for the miss, and the cache ratio controls how often that happens.

Takeaway: Grow the compute with the corpus, and warm latency stays flat. Only the queries that miss the cache get slower as the corpus grows.

The throughput test sent hybrid queries straight to Lakebase Postgres, without the app, so it measures the database alone. It opened 1, 4, 16, or 64 connections to Lakebase Postgres at the same time. Each connection sent a query, waited for the answer, and then sent the next one. The chart shows the total number of queries per second across all connections. When a line goes flat, more connections do not finish more queries. Lakebase Postgres is then at its limit, and each query waits longer instead. The load generator's own CPU stayed near zero, so Lakebase Postgres set every number.

On the 4M corpus the skewed mix reached about 4 queries per second at 2 CU, 15 at 8 CU, and 65 at 16 CU. At 64 connections, the median wait for one query was 14.5 s at 2 CU, 5.2 s at 8 CU, and 343 ms at 16 CU. The uniform mix at 16 CU peaked at 30 queries per second, because it never reuses a page. Throughput scales with the compute size and the cache ratio together.

Read these as the cost of cache misses under load. Most queries in a real app repeat or cluster, so the warm hit rate, not the uniform mix, sets steady-state capacity.

Takeaway: More CU buys throughput twice, with more CPU and a larger cache. Going from 8 CU to 16 CU raised the skewed throughput from 15 to 65 queries per second.

The lakebase_ann index is approximate. Recall@10 is the share of the true 10 nearest passages, from an exact search over all vectors, that the index also returns. The index splits the vectors into partitions (IVF), and lakebase_ann.probes sets how many partitions a query reads. Recall@10 barely moved with the corpus size at the default probe count: 0.74 at 1M, 0.75 at 2M, and 0.75 at 4M. More probes trade latency for recall.

With the default index at 4M, the default 109 probes gave a recall@10 of 0.74 in 3 ms, and 2,000 probes gave 0.95 in 49 ms. An index built with build_mode = 'quality' raised recall at every probe count: 0.80 at the default probes in 3 ms, and 0.97 at 2,000 probes in about the same time as the default build. Its build took 52 minutes at 16 CU. Raising lakebase_ann.epsilon to 4, the highest value it accepted in our tests, added less than 0.3 points.[9] Recall depends on the data and the embedding model, so measure it on your own data and pick the probe count your app needs. Lakebase Search supports a single index of over 1 billion vectors.[1]

Takeaway: Build the vector index with build_mode = 'quality'. At the default probes it raised recall@10 from 0.74 to 0.80 in about 3 ms, and at 500 probes it reached 0.91 in 13 ms, which takes 1,000 probes and 20 ms on the default build. The cost is the build time: 52 minutes for 4M passages at 16 CU. Raise the probes only if your app needs more recall.

Lakebase cost follows use. A suspended compute incurs no compute cost, and storage is billed separately. Lakebase was about 1% of the Slide Hub 30-day bill. Slide Hub is an internal app, and a slower first search after 5 idle minutes is acceptable for its users, so its production database scales to zero when nobody searches.

The scale evaluation was cheap. The self-hosted embedding of the whole corpus took 2.95 GPU-hours, against $48.87 for the model-serving endpoint. One in-region load ramp ran for 14 minutes and cost $0.13 at list price: $0.11 for the app and $0.02 for Lakebase Postgres, which autoscaled between 0.5 and 1 CU and used 0.21 CU-hours. Up to 1,000 users the ramp served 109,602 requests without errors. The cells ran at 0.5 to 16 CU and suspended between runs. In our workspace's billing tables, one CU-hour is 0.213 DBU: about $0.085 at the Premium list price and $0.11 at the Enterprise list price in AWS US East.

Takeaway: Lakebase Postgres bills compute only while it runs. The 14-minute load test used $0.02 of Lakebase Postgres compute, and that compute cost was about 1% of the Slide Hub 30-day bill. For production, set the minimum to 0.5 CU instead of scaling to zero. At list price that costs about $31 to $40 a month, and searches no longer wait about 1 s for the compute to wake or start with an empty cache.[11] Let dev and test branches scale to zero.

MIRACL English is open. The corpus is Apache-2.0, and its passages come from Wikipedia under CC BY-SA. The embedding model gte-large-en-v1.5 is Apache-2.0.This post reports aggregate metrics only. The same test runs with any 1024-dimension model: swap the embedding step, keep the table, the indexes, and the search.

Think of Lakebase Postgres as a reader at a desk in front of a large bookshelf.

  • The bookshelf is storage, and the desk is the cache. Pages on the desk are fast to read. Pages on the shelf take a walk, about 0.3 ms each.
  • Make the desk as large as the books you use. When the cache is about as large as the vector index, almost every page is on the desk, and a vector search takes milliseconds.
  • More CU gives a larger desk and more hands. That makes each search faster and lets Lakebase Postgres answer more searches at the same time.
  • Ask for fewer books. A search that takes 200 candidates instead of 1,000 carries about a third of the pages and keeps 9 of the top 10 results.
  • Sort the shelves well, then choose how many to search. An index built in quality mode returns 8 of the true 10 nearest passages at the default probes in 3 ms, and 97 of 100 with 2,000 probes in about 50 ms.
  • The app has its own desk. Once Lakebase Postgres is fast, the app’s workers become the limit. Then give the app more workers. More Lakebase Postgres CU does not help at that point.
  • You do not need the whole library on the desk. Lakebase Postgres reads the rest from storage. It is slower, but it works, and the cache ratio tells you how often it happens.
  • You pay for the desk only while someone reads. When nobody searches, Lakebase Postgres can suspend and bill only storage; in Slide Hub it was about 1% of the 30-day bill. In production, keep a small desk open: 0.5 CU costs about $31 to $40 a month and avoids the cold start.

Databricks has three searches, and each one fits a different job. Pick the one that sits next to your data.

  • Lakebase Search runs inside the app's Postgres database. Use it when the search must live next to the app's own tables and see each write at once.
  • AI Search, formerly Vector Search, is a managed search service over Lakehouse tables in Unity Catalog. It keeps its index in sync with a Delta or Iceberg table and can create the embeddings for you. Use it for RAG, agents, and recommendations over Lakehouse data.
  • Full-text search indexes (Beta) speed up SQL queries on managed Delta and Iceberg tables. The search and isearch functions use the index to skip files that cannot contain a match, so log and keyword lookups read less data. They filter rows and do not rank results for a search bar.

Slide Hub runs all of this in one Lakebase Postgres database: the app data, the vector index, and the keyword index. Start with the Lakebase Search docs, then run the same test against your own data.

entries.summary: Databricks serverless compute is fully managed, intelligent, and versionless, allowing...
entries.content:
Serverless networking made simple

by Alex Esibov, Manish Bansal, Stanley Wang, Justin Ly and Vijay Raja

  • What is PNG — Private Network Gateway (PNG) is a Databricks-managed gateway that enables easy and secure connectivity from serverless workloads to your private networks and resources at scale.
  • What does it solve — PNG eliminates operational burden by replacing individual connections with one network-level setup — you configure it once, and your existing routes, DNS, and firewall rules decide what's reachable.
  • How can you get started — PNG is now available in Public Preview on Azure and in Private Preview on AWS. Support for Google Cloud is currently in development and coming soon.

Databricks serverless compute is fully managed, intelligent, and versionless, allowing users to focus on solving business problems rather than sizing, tuning, and managing clusters and infrastructure. However, for many teams, the high-friction step that remained was networking: giving serverless compute a private path to databases, applications, and systems inside their own networks. In our customer interviews, more than 75% said their current network configuration and the complexity of dealing with network changes was the main reason specific workloads stayed on classic compute instead of moving to serverless.

Today, we are announcing the public preview of Private Network Gateway (PNG) on Azure, and private preview on AWS. PNG gives your serverless workloads one connection into your network, and from there, you control access to everything your network can already reach.

  • Simplify ingestion across your private databases: use Lakeflow Connect on serverless compute to ingest from supported databases across your VNet/VPC and connected on-premises environments
  • Connect AI agents to private services: An agent you build on Databricks can call a private MCP server you host
  • Use your own package repositories: Serverless can install Python libraries from a private PyPI, Artifactory, or Nexus repository inside your network
  • Route egress through your own firewall: Send traffic through your existing firewall or content inspection service, so egress is filtered and logged natively with your own tools
  • Keep a consistent, customer-owned source IP: Your SaaS apps like Salesforce, can see a source IP that belongs to you

Each of these used to require coordinated deployment between networking, security, and admin teams, and multiple new deployments like load balancers and proxy VMs. With PNG, you configure one connection, and the resources your network can reach become reachable from serverless. PNG scales by network, not by endpoint.

Private Network Gateway has significantly simplified how we connect serverless compute to data sources on Azure and on-premises — no more standing up a private link service and load balancer for every connection. It also brings real flexibility to our serverless operations: we can reuse an existing workspace subnet, which makes firewall approvals easier, while still controlling exactly which destinations are reachable.—Fabiano Seki, Tech Lead, Data Engineering, Banco Bradesco

Classic compute runs inside your own virtual network, so reaching your data is straightforward: you peer the networks using standard cloud primitives. In contrast, serverless runs in a Databricks-managed network, which, on one hand removes the operational overhead, but it also means your private resources need an explicit path.

Serverless Private Link provides that path, and it remains the right tool for cloud-managed services like AWS S3, or Azure Data Lake Storage. But for resources you host and manage, like databases, Kafka clusters, or internal APIs, connecting often meant a separate private endpoint, load balancer, and proxy VM for each resource — plus back-and-forth coordination between your Databricks admin, cloud admin, and network security team. For a handful of resources, this may be manageable. But when a team needs serverless to access dozens of databases, APIs, and internal services; across VNets, peered networks, and on-premises environments, the per-resource approach quickly becomes a bottleneck, making it painful, slow, and manually intensive.

The setup is easy and straightforward: You delegate one subnet in your virtual network to Databricks and PNG establishes a managed, encrypted gateway from serverless compute into that subnet. You configure the gateway inside a Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC), the same account-level object you already use for serverless networking. You can then attach the NCC to your workspaces, and supported serverless workloads can reach the private destinations you allow.

There are no gateway VMs for you to deploy, patch, or scale in your network. Databricks creates and runs the gateway for you. You keep control of your network.

Before PNG, enabling private connectivity for Databricks Serverless required significant network setup and coordination. PNG simplified the whole process, reduced operational overhead, and helped us run jobs faster—making serverless much easier to integrate into our existing environment.—Primož Gale, Lead Technical Architect, NLB

PNG keeps the network boundary with you:

  • Your gateway is yours: it provides a dedicated path into your network, not a shared appliance carrying other customers' traffic. Isolation is enforced via encapsulation and network security rules.
  • The gateway enforces workspace-level access controls before any traffic leaves.
  • Beyond the subnet, your route tables, network security groups, DNS resolvers, and security appliances decide what serverless can reach, the same way they do for the rest of your network.

You choose how much traffic PNG carries, through two modes:

  • specific_destinations
    sends only the fully qualified domain names you list through PNG. All other traffic keeps its normal path. Use this when you want precise control over which resources serverless can reach.
  • all_traffic
    routes outbound traffic through your network, except anything matching a more-specific Private Link or service-endpoint path, which keeps its native route. Use this mode to inspect broad egress through your own firewall, or to send it out through your own IP addresses.

PNG is additive. It sits alongside the private connectivity and egress controls you already use for Databricks and does not change them, so you can enable or remove it without affecting your existing setup.

Before Private Network Gateway, managing secrets and network connectivity for serverless workloads required multiple integrations and ongoing coordination. Today, with PNG, we can securely access internal services directly and centrally manage outbound traffic through our existing controls, making operations simpler, faster, and easier to govern.—Michel Schwandner, Platform Engineer, Julius Blum GmbH

Private Network Gateway is now available in Public Preview on Azure, and in Private Preview on AWS. Support for Google Cloud is in development.

Get started today:

  • Private Network Gateway - Azure documentation
  • For AWS, contact your Databricks account team to discuss enrollment

entries.title: A practical guide to real-time analytics in 2026
entries.summary: Data has always been central to business decision-making, and most analytical workloads...
entries.content:
Most organizations don't need a separate real-time serving layer. Learn how to evaluate real-time workloads and deliver millisecond analytics directly on your lakehouse.

  • Real-time analytics delivers insights within milliseconds of an event occurring. Understanding three dimensions (freshness, latency, and concurrency) helps you identify where real-time creates measurable business value.
  • Organizations typically bolt on specialized serving layers when they need to analyze data in real-time, creating duplicated data, fragile pipelines, and fragmented governance.
  • A lakehouse approach delivers millisecond query performance and high concurrency directly on governed data. Learn how to evaluate real-time analytics workloads, see common use cases across industries, and find best practices for building and optimizing real-time analytics at scale.

Data has always been central to business decision-making, and most analytical workloads aren't particularly latency-sensitive. But a growing set of use cases — real-time BI dashboards, operational monitoring, logging, live reporting — need insights that reflect what's happening right now. This is real-time analytics, and it's becoming a critical capability.

"Real-time" can mean many things. Message buses move data between systems. Stream processors transform data as it arrives. Those systems are a part of most modern data architectures, and many are already sources of data in lakehouses and analytical engines today.

The complexity compounds when it's time to actually query and analyze that data in real time — which usually means spinning up a specialized serving engine like Apache Druid, Apache Pinot, or ClickHouse, each with its own data copies, pipelines, and governance. That's a lot of overhead for what should be another analytical workload with a different latency profile.

There's a better way. Real-time analytics should be a feature of the lakehouse where you already run your other analytical workloads. Learn what real-time analytics actually means, how to identify which workloads truly need it, and how a lakehouse approach delivers fast, governed, real-time insights without the architectural sprawl. 

Real-time data analytics enables organizations to analyze data and deliver insights with minimal delay after events occur. But "real-time" isn't a single requirement. A customer-facing recommendation engine and an executive dashboard both need current data, but they have very different expectations for speed and scale.

Rather than treating real-time as a binary, it's more useful to evaluate workloads across three measurable dimensions.

Freshness measures how recent your data is when it's queried: the time between when an event occurs and when it becomes available for analysis. A fraud detection system may need transactions available within a second. An operations dashboard refreshed every minute may still deliver timely, useful insights.

Latency measures how quickly the system responds after a query is submitted. A dashboard might display data that's only seconds old, but if every query takes several seconds to return, users still won't experience real-time analytics. Low latency matters most for interactive dashboards, customer-facing applications, APIs, and AI agents.

Concurrency measures how many users, applications, or processes can access data simultaneously without performance degrading. Internal BI tools may support hundreds of concurrent users. Customer-facing applications, embedded analytics, and AI agents can generate thousands of simultaneous requests.

Together, these three dimensions define the requirements of any real-time workload and help you determine whether real-time capabilities are actually needed.

The simplest way to think about it: does your workload need insights in milliseconds to seconds, or can it wait minutes to hours? Real-time analytics covers the first category — live dashboards, customer recommendations, operational monitoring, and logging. Batch analytics covers the second — historical reporting, forecasting, and scheduled analysis.

Approach

Typical latency

Best for

Tradeoffs

Real-time

Milliseconds to seconds

Live BI dashboards, customer recommendations, operational monitoring, logging

Higher performance requirements; demands low-latency serving

Batch

Minutes to hours or daily

Historical reporting, forecasting, financial close

Most efficient, but insights are delayed

If you run both — and most organizations do — you shouldn't need multiple tools, multiple governance models, and multiple security postures to do it. You should be able to run real-time and batch analytics from one place, on one copy of your data, with one set of controls.

A simple qualification framework can help teams determine where real-time analytics delivers the most impact:

  • What business outcome does real-time enable? Real-time is most valuable when faster access to insights drives a meaningful action or improves a user experience. If acting on fresher data doesn't create measurable impact, batch processing is likely sufficient.
  • What are the workload requirements? Evaluate the level of freshness, latency, and concurrency required. Workloads with immediate decision-making needs, interactive experiences, or large numbers of concurrent users are strong candidates.
  • How critical is real-time performance? Determine whether delays in data availability or query response would impact revenue, customer experience, or operational efficiency.
  • How will the data be consumed? Insights used by analysts have different requirements than data powering customer-facing applications, operational systems, or AI agents. Consumption patterns shape how you design and scale analytics.

The need for real-time analytics looks different across industries, but the underlying patterns are the same: organizations need to query and explore fresh data without the overhead of maintaining a separate real-time infrastructure alongside their existing analytics platform.

Financial services. Faster analysis means less financial loss, and real-time risk visibility supports better decisions under pressure. Fraud detection, trading analytics, and risk monitoring demand millisecond-to-second latency with high concurrency across analysts, applications, and automated systems.

Retail and ecommerce. Shoppers won't wait for yesterday's recommendations. Personalization, dynamic pricing, and inventory optimization need seconds-to-minutes freshness with high concurrency across customer-facing applications, translating directly to higher conversion rates and fewer stockouts.

Manufacturing. Factory floors generate enormous volumes of sensor data, and the value drops fast. IoT monitoring, predictive maintenance, and operational analytics depend on near real-time processing of high-volume data streams to catch equipment failures before they cause downtime.

Healthcare. Delayed data can mean delayed interventions. Patient monitoring, operational analytics, and clinical insights require seconds-to-minutes latency with concurrent access across care teams and applications, supporting timely decisions that improve patient outcomes.

Technology and SaaS. Product telemetry, customer analytics, and AI-powered features generate constant demand for fresh data at millisecond-to-second latency across large numbers of concurrent users. Companies that act on product signals in real time ship better features, resolve incidents faster, and deliver more responsive experiences.

Organizations have typically met real-time needs by adding specialized serving layers alongside existing data platforms. These systems solve specific problems but create new ones: duplicated data, additional pipelines to maintain, fragmented governance, and operational overhead that grows with every new real-time workload.

As real-time becomes core to everyday analytics and AI, this approach doesn't scale. Managing multiple copies of the same data across separate real-time systems like ClickHouse, StarRocks, Apache Druid, Apache Pinot, and SingleStore increases both complexity and cost.

The lakehouse architecture combines the best elements of a data lake and a data warehouse to unify analytical workloads on a single, open foundation. By offering scalable storage, high-performance compute, open table formats, and centralized governance, organizations can support BI, data engineering, and AI workloads without maintaining separate data silos.

The next evolution extends this foundation to real-time workloads natively, delivering millisecond performance and high concurrency directly from governed lakehouse data without requiring a separate serving layer. This means organizations can support real-time analytics alongside traditional data warehousing on the same platform, with the same governance, using the same data.

On Databricks, Lakehouse//RT was built to close this gap. It's powered by Reyden, a purpose-built compute engine that enables real-time analytics performance directly on governed lakehouse data, with no separate serving layer required.

  • Millisecond query performance for operational analytics, application serving, interactive BI, and more
  • High concurrency at scale, supporting thousands of simultaneous users, applications, and AI agents without performance degradation
  • No data duplication, because it queries the same governed tables your analytics and AI workloads already use
  • Unified governance, so real-time data is subject to the same access controls, lineage, and quality standards as everything else on Databricks via Unity Catalog

In practice, this means a retail team can power real-time personalization from the same data their analysts use for weekly reporting. A financial services firm can run fraud detection queries alongside risk modeling without maintaining parallel infrastructure. And an AI agent can retrieve fresh, governed context in milliseconds from the same tables that feed the company's dashboards.

Lakehouse//RT doesn't replace your existing Lakehouse setup. It extends it, giving you real-time capabilities on the data foundation you've already built.

Real-time performance depends on more than selecting the right compute. How you organize, query, and maintain data plays an equally important role.

Optimize data layout and table design. Use managed tables to simplify data management. Apply intelligent data layout strategies like liquid clustering to optimize data access patterns. Leverage automatic optimization to reduce manual maintenance.

Design efficient query patterns. Real-time workloads require frequent queries against fresh data, making query efficiency critical. Minimize unnecessary data scans, select only the data required for each workload, and optimize frequently accessed queries based on actual usage patterns.

Plan for concurrency from the start. Consider expected query volume, response-time requirements, and usage patterns early. Real-time workloads often serve many users, applications, and processes simultaneously, so design for consistent performance as demand grows.

Design for downstream applications and AI. Real-time analytics increasingly powers experiences beyond dashboards. Applications, APIs, and AI agents depend on timely access to governed data. Understanding how data will be consumed helps you design workloads that meet both analytical and operational requirements.

Monitor and optimize over time. Real-time workloads evolve as usage patterns, data volumes, and business requirements change. Continuous monitoring helps you identify opportunities to improve performance, manage costs, and maintain reliability at scale.

You don't need to make every workload real-time overnight. A phased approach works best:

  • Identify high-value workloads where faster access to data creates measurable business impact
  • Evaluate requirements across freshness, latency, and concurrency
  • Start with a unified foundation that supports real-time alongside existing analytics and AI workloads
  • Optimize and expand as you validate performance and discover new real-time opportunities

As AI agents, customer-facing applications, and operational systems continue to evolve, the ability to deliver governed, high-performance analytics directly where data lives will become increasingly important. Organizations that build on a unified, flexible foundation will be better positioned to adapt as new real-time opportunities emerge.

Learn more about Lakehouse//RT and connect with your account team to explore what new opportunities you can unlock with real-time analytics directly on your Lakehouse.

Keep reading:

Frequently asked questions about real-time analytics

Real-time analytics is the practice of analyzing data and delivering insights within seconds or milliseconds of an event occurring. Unlike batch analytics, which processes data on a schedule (hourly, daily, or weekly), real-time analytics makes fresh data available for queries, dashboards, applications, and automated systems as soon as it arrives. The specific speed requirements vary by workload: live customer recommendations may need sub-second responses, while a live operations dashboard refreshed every few seconds can still qualify as real-time.

Evaluate your workload across three dimensions: freshness (how recent the data needs to be when queried), latency (how fast the system needs to respond), and concurrency (how many users or applications will query simultaneously). If acting on fresher data drives a measurable business outcome, if users or applications need responses in milliseconds, or if thousands of concurrent requests are expected, real-time analytics is likely a fit. If none of these conditions apply, batch processing is usually more efficient.

Not necessarily. Organizations have traditionally added specialized serving layers (such as ClickHouse, Apache Druid, or Apache Pinot) alongside their data warehouse to meet real-time requirements. This approach works but creates trade-offs: duplicated data, additional pipelines, fragmented governance, and operational overhead that grows with each new real-time workload. A lakehouse architecture can support real-time analytics natively on the same governed data your analytics and AI workloads already use, eliminating the need for a separate serving layer.

Real-time analytics is used across industries wherever timely data drives better decisions or experiences. In financial services, it powers trading analytics, and risk monitoring. In retail and ecommerce, it enables personalization, dynamic pricing, and inventory optimization. Manufacturing teams use it for IoT monitoring and predictive maintenance. Healthcare organizations apply it to patient monitoring and clinical decision support. Technology and SaaS companies rely on it for product telemetry, customer analytics, and AI-powered applications.

The most important factors are query latency (can it return results in milliseconds?), concurrency (can it handle thousands of simultaneous users and applications?), data freshness (how quickly does new data become queryable?), and governance (are real-time workloads subject to the same access controls and data quality standards as everything else?). Also consider whether the platform requires you to duplicate data into a separate system or whether it can deliver real-time performance on your existing data foundation. Platforms that unify real-time and traditional analytics reduce complexity and long-term cost.

A lakehouse approach lets organizations run real-time analytics on the same platform, data, and governance model they already use for traditional analytics and AI. Instead of bolting on a separate real-time database with its own ingestion pipelines and access controls, a lakehouse extends your existing foundation with real-time capabilities. This means one copy of the data, one set of governance policies, and no additional infrastructure to manage. On Databricks, Lakehouse//RT delivers millisecond query performance and high concurrency directly on governed lakehouse data.

entries.content:
Learn about the latest innovations in Lakeflow Designer coming to your workspace this fall

by Jason Messer, Emanuel Zgraggen, V Maharajh, Kyrylo Bakumenko, Xiao Yan and Matt Jones

  • New and enhanced operators support data cleaning, deduplication, quality checks, more flexible joins, and parameterized inputs and outputs.
  • Expanded output options and canvas improvements add materialized views, table merges, file exports, visual version history, and live cursor presence.
  • Upcoming features include Databricks Apps integration, data profiling on full outputs, a Custom Report operator, and native migration tooling with Lakebridge.

We launched Lakeflow Designer to general availability in June, and since then, over 3,000 customers have used it to address one of the biggest bottlenecks in working with data: the technical barrier to entry. Teams migrating from legacy self-service data preparation tools have streamlined governance, simplified their data stacks, accelerated their path to production, and cut costs dramatically. With consumption-based pricing and no per-user licensing fees, we’ve seen many customers reduce their spend on no-code tooling by 90% after adopting Lakeflow Designer.

Working closely with these customers has helped us identify ways to make Designer even more useful. Our latest updates bring new no-code operators, enhancements to existing operators, more output options, and an improved canvas for building and managing larger workflows.

Built directly in Databricks, Lakeflow Designer is a visual, no-code, AI-native experience for data preparation and analytics. It lets analysts, domain experts, and other less technical users prepare and explore data through a drag-and-drop canvas and natural language.

Here are some of our favorite enhancements we've made to Lakeflow Designer over the last 4 months.

Genie Code, Python, and SQL operators have always made Designer flexible. However, we heard from early customers that they wanted more no-code ways to handle common tasks like deduplication, data cleaning, and data quality checks.

Prepare operator: Clean and standardize data

Clean and standardize your data with the Prepare operator. Change text case, convert data types, replace values, apply formulas, and more, all in a single operator. Learn more about Prepare.

Unique operator: Remove duplicate records

Quickly remove duplicates across the entire dataset or a selected set of columns. Set an order to control which record you keep, such as the most recently updated record for each customer. Learn more about Unique.

Guardrails operator: Add data quality checks

Add data quality checks directly to your workflow with Guardrails. Check for missing values, duplicates, unexpected values, and more, then choose how failures affect the workflow: continue with passing rows, block the passed output, or stop execution. Learn more about Guardrails.

We’ve expanded existing operators to better handle advanced use cases and branching.

Split and multi-join

The Join operator now provides separate outputs for matched, left unmatched, and right unmatched rows by default, allowing you to branch workflows and trigger alerts on unexpected values. It also supports joining more than two tables in a single operator. Learn more about Join.

Dynamic column selection

Select columns by data type, name pattern, or formula, so your workflow adapts as the input schema changes. For example, keep every column whose name starts with 

sales_
, including new matching columns added later. Learn more about Select.

Parameterize inputs and outputs

Source and Output operators now support parameters in their configuration, letting you change these values without reconfiguring the operator. Parameters can be overridden based on individual schedules, such as runs in test and production environments. Learn more about parameters.

Branching in the Filter operator

The Filter operator now has separate outputs for rows that match your conditions and rows that don't. Use both outputs to build separate processing paths from a single filter. Learn more about Filter.

The Output operator now gives you more ways to save results, update existing data, and create files for downstream use.

Create materialized views

Write your results as a materialized view in Unity Catalog for fast computation in downstream processes like AI/BI Dashboards or even other visual data prep files. The view refreshes automatically when your visual data prep runs. Learn more about materialized view outputs.

Merge into existing tables

Keep an existing table up to date by merging results using the keys you specify. Matching records are updated, and new records are inserted. You can also append results to the end of an existing table. Learn more about table outputs.

Write directly to files

Write CSV, Excel, or JSON files directly to Unity Catalog volumes. For Excel outputs, you can also write dynamically to different worksheets. Learn more about file outputs.

We've updated the canvas to make larger workflows easier to navigate, understand, and maintain.

Navigate larger workflows with a visually redesigned canvas

The canvas has a refreshed design with more visual contrast, larger connection targets, and clearer cues for unconfigured operators and missing inputs. We've also improved scrolling and panning on canvases with 1000s of operators, making large workflows more responsive to navigate.

Find operators with a searchable table of contents

Find any operator using the new searchable table of contents, then select it to jump to its location on the canvas. You can also expand its 

Generated code
section to inspect the underlying code.

Review workflow changes with a visual version history

See what changed between versions directly on the canvas. Version history now highlights operators that were added, removed, or modified, making workflow changes easier to review. Learn more about version history.

Follow collaborators with live cursor presence

Live cursor presence lets you collaborate and follow what coworkers are doing when you're working in the same visual data prep file.

We are continuing to invest in making Lakeflow Designer the best self-service data preparation and automation tool to work with data. The following are a few upcoming improvements we’re excited about.

Databricks Apps integration

We're integrating Designer with Databricks Apps so authors can share their work with non-technical users through a simple app interface. Users will be able to configure inputs, run the workflow, and view results without viewing the underlying workflow.

Data profiling on the full output

We're expanding Designer's existing data profiling capabilities so you can run a profile across all data returned by an operator and view the results directly in the output table header.

Create custom reports from multiple outputs with the Report operator

A new Report operator will let you combine results from multiple outputs with custom graphics like company logos. You'll be able to save reports directly to the workspace or deliver them via email through a native notification operator.

Native migration tooling with Lakebridge

Native migration tooling powered by Databricks Lakebridge will let you bulk migrate workflows from legacy self-service data preparation tools directly into Lakeflow Designer.

Is Lakeflow Designer available in Databricks Free Edition?

Yes. Select Visual Data Prep in the left navigation to get started in Free Edition.

How is Lakeflow Designer priced?

There are no per-user licenses or separate licensing fees for Lakeflow Designer. You only pay for the compute you use.

Where can I see the generated code?

You can view the underlying code for any operator by opening the table of contents and expanding 

Generated code
. You can also export the entire file through File > Export to inspect the underlying code.

Does Lakeflow Designer work with Git?

Yes. Place your Lakeflow Designer files in a Databricks Git folder to track changes and sync with your Git provider. Each file contains both the visual layout and the underlying Python code, so both are versioned together.

Can I use Lakeflow Designer for HIPAA workloads?

Yes. Lakeflow Designer supports HIPAA workloads in workspaces configured to meet Databricks HIPAA requirements, including the required compliance controls and an active Business Associate Agreement (BAA). See the HIPAA documentation for requirements and regional availability.

Lakeflow Designer is generally available in all Databricks workspaces. To try it, click + New in the top left of the workspace and select Visual data prep.

To learn more, check out these other resources:

  • Read our Public Preview announcement for an overview of what Lakeflow Designer is and how teams are using it.
  • Watch a demo video.
  • Check out the documentation.
  • We'd love to hear what you think, especially about the design ideas in this post. Reach us at designer-feedback@databricks.com.
  • Want to work on these problems with us? We're hiring.

Debuts with the highest initial placement of any new vendor in the Magic Quadrant’’s 20+ year history.

by Chao Cai, Kayli Berlin and Miranda Luna

  • Databricks achieved the highest debut performance ever in the more than 20 year history of the Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Analytics and BI Platforms.
  • Databricks was recognized as a Visionary, achieving one of the highest scores for "Completeness of Vision" among all evaluated vendors.
  • Explore how Databricks AI/BI, Genie, and the Data + AI Platform are driving the market shift toward converged platforms, agentic analytics, and centralized semantics.

We are incredibly excited to announce that Databricks has made its inaugural appearance in the Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Analytics and Business Intelligence (ABI) Platforms 2026. Databricks debuted in the quadrant as a "Visionary". We also achieved one of the highest "Completeness of Vision" scores among all vendors evaluated.

This marks the highest debut performance any vendor has ever had in the 20+ year history of this Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ report. We believe this recognition validates our core thesis: the fundamental nature of BI has changed, and the future belongs to data platforms that inherently fuse analytics with enterprise AI. Legacy BI tools were built for a different era: one defined by rigid data models and heavy data extracts that tied data teams up with answering basic questions, rather than freeing them to drive high-value, strategic analysis. The days of locking data into proprietary BI silos to build backward-looking dashboards have already ended.

Gartner’s Hype Cycle for Analytics and Business Intelligence highlights this massive change in the industry. We see our strong placement in the Magic Quadrant as a direct result of our ability to deliver on three major trends reshaping businesses today:

  • Data & AI Platform Convergence: Bringing different tools together into a single platform reduces everyday complexity, streamlines workflows, and makes it easier to scale AI infrastructure. This union enables the global boom in AI adoption by ensuring company-wide data use is consistent and governed.
  • Agentic Analytics: AI agents are transforming data management, analysis, and decision-making. By automating manual workflows, they help organizations move faster and drive greater business value.
  • Semantics at the Core: A unified, governed semantic layer gives every human and agent the same definitions, context, and rules. It is critical to safely scale autonomous agents and agent-to-agent workflows. Without it, conflicting interpretations create too much risk of error.

For decades, traditional BI forced a bad tradeoff: copy data into separate systems—fracturing governance and analyzing stale information—or pay extra for bespoke engines to query it in place. Augmented BI did not change that foundation; it simply layered forecasts and anomaly detection onto the same incomplete data picture.

Truly agentic BI requires eliminating every information silo so agents can reason over the full, governed context. Agents are only as smart as the part of the picture they can access, and incomplete context creates unreliable answers. That is why Databricks integrates BI directly into the lakehouse. With Genie and AI/BI, agents work from the same complete, governed source of truth—without extracts, duplicated data, or a separate BI layer.

Databricks’ agentic analytics offering eliminates manual bottlenecks by automating complex workflows, empowering teams to move faster from insight to autonomous action and drive significantly greater business value. Databricks AI/BI pushes business intelligence beyond basic queries into dynamic, action-oriented workflows. Genie One, our data-smart AI coworker, seamlessly connects insights to smart actions, eliminating the manual steps typically required between finding a data point and acting on it. Furthermore, Genie Agents allow teams to turn simple prompts into shareable, independent agents capable of reasoning through both structured data tables and messy, unstructured documents. By taking autonomous action to manage schedules, generate documents, and execute complex multi-step workflows across your business tools, these capabilities drastically reduce manual toil.

Trusted AI and BI start with a shared understanding of your business. Unity Catalog Business Semantics lets you define metrics, dimensions, relationships, and business terms once, then govern and apply them consistently across dashboards, analytics, and agents. Genie Ontology builds on that foundation by automatically organizing context from data, queries, dashboards, pipelines, and connected tools into a living map of how your business works. Together, they help Genie know where to look, what to trust, and how to answer complex questions with complete, governed business context.

BI has already changed. It is no longer just about building dashboards and reports in advance for a specific part of the business. The new model is dynamic and proactive. Insights are pushed to you, not just pulled when you ask for them. Anyone can dig deeper from a high-level trend down to the real truth behind it, and AI agents make sure every answer tells the full story.

That new world is exactly where we are ahead with Genie and Databricks AI/BI. Business users rely on it every day to see key trends, understand what changed and why, and decide what to do about it instantly. By bringing insights directly to where you work—whether that is through mobile apps, Slack, Microsoft Teams, or custom AI assistants—we are truly putting data in the hands of everyone in the company.

We are grateful to the thousands of customers who have partnered with us to push the limits of what is possible with their data. Being named a Visionary with the highest debut performance in the history of the Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Analytics and BI Platforms is an incredible milestone, and it is only the beginning.

Ready to see the future of AI-driven analytics in action? Learn more about AI/BI here.

entries.content:
Building University Recruiting in India

by Clara Kurian and Andrea Fernández

  • Get an insider look at Databricks' strategic growth and campus recruiting initiatives across India.
  • Learn about the inaugural Bengaluru intern program and what it signals for the company's regional expansion.
  • Understand what Data and AI companies look for when evaluating early career talent in India.

Brickster Voices is a series that spotlights the people who make our work possible. Through personal career journeys, behind-the-scenes looks at impactful projects and a glimpse into how we work together, these stories offer a window into life at Databricks. Whether you're exploring new opportunities, curious about our work in data and AI or simply inspired by stories of growth and collaboration, Brickster Voices invites you to get to know the individuals driving our mission forward.

As part of our Brickster Voices series, we sat down with Clara Kurian, Sr. Recruiter for University Recruiting in APJ. Clara is Databricks' first university recruiter for the region. With Databricks' $250M+ investment in India and plans for 50% workforce expansion, Clara's work sits at the center of one of the company's growth stories.

What does Databricks' investment in India look like on the ground?

Clara: From where I sit in Bengaluru, the investment doesn't feel like a headline; it feels like something you can see and feel day to day. India isn't being treated as a satellite office or a back-end function. It's a strategic hub. Since 2022, India has grown +270%, backed by a strong leadership presence that has expanded +350% across all business units. That scale is visible across every function: Engineering has grown 14x, while our Field Engineering & Professional Services (FE & PS) teams have scaled by +260%.

This is the kind of moment that doesn't come around often. You're not stepping into something already built and set in its ways; you're helping shape what it becomes. For early career talent especially, that's rare: the chance to grow alongside the organization, take on real scope early, and genuinely influence the trajectory rather than just inherit it. The energy here reminds me of why I joined in the first place, a mix of momentum and possibility. And now it's happening at scale, right here in India.

What does Databricks' community investment in India signal to candidates?

C: What it really shows is that Databricks isn't just here to hire, it's here to be part of the community. A lot of companies show up when they have roles to fill, but here it's much more than that. Whether it's the engineering networking events that bring in senior leaders from across the tech ecosystem, the Bharat Bricks Hacks Hackathons we run across the IITs and IISc, or the sponsorship of Bengaluru Tech Week. None of it is about one hire. It's about actually investing in the people, campuses, and ideas that are shaping tech in India.

For candidates, especially early in their career, it means you're joining somewhere that's genuinely embedded into what's happening around it, not off on the sidelines, but right in the middle of it.

You currently run Databricks' first structured India Intern Program with 51 interns. What was your vision?

C: The vision was straightforward: I wanted interns to leave feeling like they'd actually been at Databricks, not just observing it from the outside. The goal wasn't just to give the 51 interns work to do, it was to give them the whole experience: the pace, the people, the culture, all of it.

We were intentional about designing moments that reflected what it's genuinely like to work here. Things like Speed Mentoring with our Engineering Leadership, so interns could learn directly from the people building the products, and actually feel comfortable enough to ask them anything. And then the fun, human side too, with activities like Sneaker Art, Pickleball socials. We wanted them to see both: the depth of the work and the culture that makes it enjoyable.

What I'm proudest of is that it felt like they were part of the team from day one, trusted with real work, surrounded by people invested in them, and getting a genuine taste of what a career here could look like. That, to me, is what giving early career talent a real shot looks like.

Where should early career candidates be building their skills?

C: My honest advice to students would be less about chasing a specific team and more about building strong fundamentals, because that's the foundation everything here is built on. If you're genuinely curious, love to keep learning, and get excited about solving hard problems with data, you'll find a place, because those are exactly the skills we're growing across the board.

The best part is the breadth. Whether your interest is deep systems and infrastructure or the applied AI side, there's real room to grow into it here, and you'd be doing it right as these teams are scaling in India.

What foundational skills or mindsets matter most to succeed in data and AI?

C: You don't need to know everything on day one. You just need a strong base and the willingness to keep building on it. But honestly, the mindset matters just as much as the skills, maybe more. Curiosity is the big one. This field moves so fast that the people who thrive are the ones who genuinely love learning and aren't afraid to say "I don't know that yet, but I'll figure it out."

I'd also add a builder mindset and critical thinking. That's a big part of the culture here.

What separates the candidates who really stand out?

C: The technical bar is almost a given. What makes someone stand out is how they show up as a person.

The ones I remember are genuinely curious. They ask real questions, they lean into problems they haven't seen before and they're comfortable saying "I don't know, but here's how I'd figure it out." That tells me far more than a perfectly rehearsed answer. The other big one is authenticity. The candidates who aren't trying to be who they think we want, but are just themselves, honest about what they know and what they're still learning. That self-awareness, plus real enthusiasm, is what sticks with me.

What drew you to Databricks, and what has kept you energized?

C: What drew me to Databricks was the growth and the potential I could see from the outside, that rare combination of a company with real momentum but still enough startup energy. What sealed it was the opportunity to build something from the ground up in the university recruiting space across APJ. The chance to shape a function from its early stages, rather than inherit something already fully formed, was exactly the kind of challenge I was looking for.

What's kept me energized is that no two days here are the same. There's always a new problem to solve, a new market nuance to navigate and genuine room to innovate, not once in a while, but every single day. That mix of ownership and constant reinvention is what makes it easy to stay excited about the work.

Can you share a moment where Databricks' values came to life?

C: For me, it shows up most clearly in how hiring actually works here. Hiring is never a solo function, it's always a partnership between multiple teams and businesses, and it only succeeds when everyone is equally invested in the outcome. What's struck me at Databricks is how genuinely that plays out. The stakeholders I work with go above and beyond to make a hire successful.

That's where "Customer Obsessed" comes to life for me. Everyone is aligned on the same goal and willing to put in the work to get there because they care about their part of it. And there's a real mutual respect in it: even as people take that ownership, they look to me as the subject matter expert and trust my judgment on how we get it done.

If you're excited by data and AI, love to learn, and want your work to matter early — this is one of the best places you could start. Check out our open roles today!

entries.content:
Using a privacy-first, judge-driven post-training pipeline on Databricks, Flo improved medical safety from 34% to approximately 61%, usefulness from 42% to 76%, and its combined medical safety and usefulness score from 16% to 47%.

by Vladislav Nedosekin, András Meczner, Julia Powell, Tejas Sundaresan and Michael Shtelma

  • Flo Health built a specialized evaluation framework to measure AI responses across both medical safety and usefulness, calibrated against clinician review.
  • Using privacy-first synthetic data and AI judges, Flo created training data without human-annotated training pairs, then used supervised fine-tuning and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to improve an open model.
  • Flo ran distributed fine-tuning on 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Databricks AI Runtime, improving medical safety from 34% to approximately 61%, usefulness from 42% to 76%, and the combined score from 16% to 47%.

For Flo Health, the bar for generative AI is unusually high. With 81 million monthly active users, the women’s health app operates at a scale where even small weaknesses in an AI system matter. Because Flo’s products deal with health and well-being, responses need to be medically safe and genuinely useful.

As Flo moved from using only traditional ML towards personalized insights powered by generative AI, the team saw the potential for a more flexible, personalized product. But relying on a single general-purpose model introduced other constraints: cost at scale, dependence on a model provider’s lifecycle, and limited ability to encode Flo’s own domain expertise. Flo’s longer-term vision was a compound AI system that could use the right model for each task while maintaining a consistent safety standard across them.

That led Flo toward fine-tuned open models and a new post-training pipeline built with Databricks. The team used AI judges and privacy-first synthetic data to turn Flo’s standards for medical safety and usefulness into a training signal, then used Databricks AI Runtime to run distributed fine-tuning on serverless NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

That approach also made sense economically at Flo’s scale. The team estimates that using tailored, fine-tuned models can reduce inference costs by an order of magnitude compared with relying on frontier model APIs, while giving Flo greater control over model behavior and lifecycle.

But before Flo could train models against its own standards, it needed a reliable way to define and measure what “good” looked like.

Flo defined two goals for its AI systems: medical safety as the foundation and usefulness as the goal. A model can avoid unsafe statements and still provide little value, or give a detailed, personalized answer while missing an important medical safeguard.

Consider a question such as, “Why is my period late?” An answer that simply tells the user to see a medical professional may be safe but not particularly useful. An answer that lists only common lifestyle causes may be more helpful, but incomplete from a medical-safety perspective. Flo wanted responses that could balance both: useful information, appropriate context, and the right safety netting.

To make that balance measurable, Flo’s medical, product, and engineering teams built an evaluation framework that decomposed medical risk into specific rubrics that could be tested consistently. For example, after identifying that responses to symptom questions could be overly reassuring, Flo created a “balanced causes” rule requiring appropriate coverage of both benign and potentially serious causes when relevant. Those rubrics were then turned into AI judges, each with a definition, grading instructions, and training cases.

Flo validated the judges against synthetic cases and anonymized cases from real-user experiments. When an AI judge disagreed with an initial human assessment, blinded clinical reviewers adjudicated the disagreement to establish ground truth. Flo then used part of those cases to refine the judges and reserved the rest to measure performance.

With the evaluation system in place, Flo could use those same judges as the reward signal for training. The final framework included 26 judges across three categories:

  • 12 medical-safety judges acted as hard constraints.
  • 6 “micro” judges evaluated more nuanced behaviors such as voice, grounding, framing, and fine-grained safety.
  • 8 usefulness criteria measured factors, including completeness, relevance, coherence, and tone.

Building a conventional human-labeled fine-tuning dataset would have required significant clinical expertise for every example. Flo concentrated its medical experts’ time on designing and calibrating the evaluation system, which could then score training candidates at scale.

The resulting pipeline generated more than 15,000 synthetic questions using privacy-first principles and created training pairs without human-annotated responses. Flo derived the inputs from model-generated or anonymously aggregated signals rather than user-written free text or identifiable information.

Clinicians remained essential to defining and validating what “safe” meant, but they no longer needed to manually label every individual training pair.

With calibrated judges and synthetic training data in place, Flo adopted a Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RTF) approach that generates multiple candidate responses during training, uses the evaluation system to identify the strongest ones, and fine-tunes the model so that quality is encoded in its weights rather than relying on expensive best-of-N search on every production request.

Flo’s workflow followed five stages:

  • Synthesize privacy-preserving questions.
  • Generate multiple candidate answers.
  • Score them across medical safety, usefulness, and behavioral criteria.
  • Select the strongest responses and build preference pairs.
  • Train with supervised fine-tuning and DPO, then rerun the judges to verify the results.

The first version of this approach exposed an important limitation: usefulness improved while medical safety remained relatively flat because the preference pairs did not distinguish sufficiently between degrees of medical quality.

Flo addressed that by adding a graded safety score. Responses that passed the binary safety gate were re-ranked according to how thoroughly they met the applicable medical criteria, creating preference pairs with a clearer medical-safety contrast.

Running this generate-score-select-train loop at scale is compute-intensive. Flo’s training stack combined Databricks AI Runtime, LLM Foundry, and Compose-RL, with MLflow used for tracking and checkpoints. AI Runtime provided the serverless GPU environment, LLM Foundry handled distributed training, and Compose-RL provided the preference-optimization layer.

For its fine-tuning run, Flo used 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with PyTorch and Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP), and ran SFT followed by DPO via LLM Foundry and Compose-RL.

That setup gave engineers on-demand GPU compute for distributed deep learning training, allowing them to move from synthetic data generation to evaluation to fine-tuning without manually standing up and configuring GPU clusters for each experiment. Keeping the surrounding data, experimentation, and ML tooling in the same environment made it easier to iterate across the full post-training workflow.

Databricks AI Runtime lets us train where our data already lives, with the reliability, security, and performance we need for large-scale model training. We can spend less time managing GPU infrastructure and more time improving the models themselves.—Vladislav Nedosekin, Director of Engineering, Data & AI Platform, Flo Health

That workflow produced measurable gains across both dimensions Flo cared about. The first model Flo evaluated scored 34% on its medical-safety benchmark and 42% on usefulness, while only 16% of responses met both criteria simultaneously.

After fine-tuning, medical safety increased to approximately 61%, usefulness reached 76%, and the combined score climbed from 16% to 47% — nearly three times the starting point.

The 47% combined score was an important milestone, but the more durable outcome was the reusable evaluation and training system Flo had built around it.

Flo can carry that system forward as the underlying models evolve. The team plans to apply it to newer open-weight models, including Gemma, Qwen, and Kimi, while preserving the medical safety and usefulness criteria it has already developed and validated.

With Databricks AI Runtime underpinning that loop, Flo can iterate on new models without rebuilding the training environment, keeping its engineers focused on medical expertise, model quality, and the user experience.
